text: Lesson 5 built a one-qubit, one-parameter circuit. Real variational models need many qubits and many parameters, arranged in a repeating structure. This lesson generalizes to that multi-parameter case and introduces the layered ansatz pattern you'll reuse for the rest of the course.

A realistic ansatz repeats two layer types. A rotation layer applies a parameterized single-qubit rotation, RY, RX, or RZ, to every qubit, each with its own independent trainable angle. An entangling layer applies two-qubit gates, most commonly CNOT, between neighboring qubits, so information from one qubit can affect another's state. Stacking rotation, then entangling, repeated L times, is the standard 'hardware-efficient ansatz,' chosen because it uses gates that are cheap to run on real NISQ hardware.

Here's the parameter count worked out. A 3-qubit ansatz with 2 layers, one RY rotation per qubit per layer, gives 3 parameters per layer times 2 layers, equal to 6 total trainable parameters. If each layer instead used two rotations per qubit, RY then RZ, the count doubles to 3 qubits times 2 rotations times 2 layers, equal to 12. This is the exact same accounting a classical neural network uses for its weight count.

Skip the entangling layers entirely and each qubit evolves completely independently, mathematically equivalent to separate single-qubit circuits running in parallel — it can never capture a pattern where two features together predict a label but neither alone does. And circuit depth, the number of sequential gate layers, is a real hardware cost, not a free modeling choice: on NISQ hardware, each additional gate is a new opportunity for a real error to corrupt the state.

Next lesson covers the parameter-shift rule, the real technique for getting an exact gradient out of a quantum circuit when all you can do is run it and measure the output, never peek inside mid-execution the way classical backpropagation does.
